newsitem.title: INDIA: India takes first steps towards term money market.
newsitem.headline: India takes first steps towards term money market.

text.p: Indian banks took their first steps towards launching a term money market this week but bankers say they do not expect to fix a benchmark rate for another year.
A handful of banks have started providing two-way quotes for near-term periods on Reuters and have confirmed stray deals.

Banks, until now exclusively dependent on the overnight call money market, began quoting for one week, one month and three months after the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) freed inter-bank borrowings from reserve requirements last Saturday.
"I do see an inter-bank term market upto three months taking off in the near term," said the head of money markets at a leading foreign bank in Bombay.
But two-thirds of the volume will be in the overnight to one week tenure, he said. "You need a good fix on the interest rate scenario (to offer quotes for three months to six months)."
"Most of us are comfortable with two weeks."

Banks have been quoting 8.0-9.0 percent for three-month money and 4.5-5.5 percent for one-month money. The market is still largely restricted to foreign and private Indian banks as India's large state-run banks need approvals for term lending.
"It (the spread in quotes) is still wide," said a bank treasurer. "The spread in developed economies is lower."
He said overnight rates would become less volatile as term borrowing evolved.
Eventually, he expected India's state-run banks with their large retail deposit base to emerge as term lenders to foreign banks, who have a weaker retail deposit base.
But the evolution of a benchmark rate -- christened MIBOR (Mumbai inter-bank offered rate) by banks and the media -- will take time, bank treasurers said.
Mumbai is the local name for Bombay, the commercial capital.
"I am pretty sure in about a year's time the benchmark will be established," Gordhan Kathuria, who retired on April 30 as chairman of the state-run Bank of India, said.

"It is an equation between local interest rates and the exchange value of a country's currency," Kathuria said. He said the Indian rupee was not yet freely convertible and domestic interest rates were till recently largely state-controlled.
"The benchmark can happen only when major banks integrate their domestic and forex treasuries. Even the State Bank of India has not done that," he said, referring to India's largest commercial bank.
A treasurer at a leading European bank said he wanted all concerned to go slow on a reference rate.

"You need depth and liquidity in the term market first," he said. "Once you have it you can ask someone -- I prefer NSE (National Stock Exchange) -- to call major players around 11 a.m. to take a reference rate as the benchmark," he said.
"I won't advocate doing anything on MIBOR for three months."
